To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have established the ability to detect Aβ ADDL at the fmol level using a dot-blot assay and have demonstrated that ADDLs are present in the brains of hAPP mice and that the levels of ADDLs are reduced in the presence of anti-Aβ antibodies.

we have developed a femtomolar immunoassay for the detection of Aβ ADDL and have demonstrated that this assay can be used to measure the time course of formation of ADDLs and to determine their presence in the hAPP-transgenic mouse brain.
we have developed a method to detect and measure ADDLs in biological samples and have shown that ADDLs can be detected and measured in hAPP transgenic mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to drug screening in Alzheimer’s disease, one based on a new understanding of the molecular basis of the disease.
defining the molecular basis for neurodegeneration in AD.
the development of a sensitive and specific immunoassay for ADDLs and the development of methods to screen drugs for inhibition of ADDL formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the assay described in this work provides a powerful and rapid means of determining the presence and quantity of Aβ ADDL and protofibrils, and of determining whether a candidate drug inhibits the assembly of neurotoxic Aβ assemblies.
we have developed a simple, robust, sensitive, and specific assay for ADDLs and their application to the screening of agents that inhibit the neurotoxicity of ADDLs.
we have developed and validated a simple and rapid assay to detect ADDLs in brain tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the methods described here provide an assay for the detection of ADDLs and protofibrils at the femtomolar range and are suitable for screening of candidate drugs for the prevention of ADDL formation in vitro and in vivo.

we have developed a method for detecting and quantifying ADDLs at femtomole levels and that we have applied this method to screen agents that inhibit neurotoxic ADDAL formation both in vivo (in transgenic mouse brain) and in vitro (in a cell culture system).

we have developed an assay that is suitable for screening agents for the treatment of AD and that we have used it to demonstrate that ADDLs are present in the brain of the hAPP transgenics and that these ADDLs may be responsible for the memory deficits observed in these mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ADDL immunoassay provides a sensitive and rapid assay for the detection of neurotoxic Aβ oligomers and can be used to screen for drugs that inhibit the formation of these neurotoxic species.

a simple dot-blot immundetection protocol can be developed to detect and quantitate the neurotoxic ADDLS and that this assay is useful for screening candidate drugs for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.
the femtomole ADDL immunoassay is a powerful and sensitive method to screen agents for their ability to inhibit ADDL formation and thus to identify potential therapeutic drugs for AD.
